items.title: 6.8.2 Sum to Infinity of Arithmetico-Geometric Series

blocks.text:
If \(|r| < 1\), then \(r^{n} \to 0\) and \(nr^{n} \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).
Therefore, (iii) reduces to

blocks.text_alt: S infinity equals a b over 1 minus r, plus d b r over 1 minus r squared

blocks.text: which is the required sum to infinity of arithmetico-geometric series.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why do the last two terms of (iii) vanish? They contain \(r^{n}\) and \(nr^{n}\) (because \([a + (n - 1)d]br^{n} = (a - d)br^{n} + d\,b\,nr^{n}\)). When \(|r| < 1\), \(r^{n}\) shrinks so fast that even \(nr^{n}\) goes to 0: for \(r = \frac{1}{2}\), \(10 \times \frac{1}{2^{10}} = \frac{10}{1024} \approx 0.0098\).
If \(|r| \ge 1\) the terms do not shrink and the series has no sum to infinity.

blocks.title: Example 19
steps:
Given: the series \(2\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 2 + 4\cdot 4 + 5\cdot 8 + \ldots\)
To find: \(S_n\), the sum of the first \(n\) terms.
Method: the first factors \(2, 3, 4, 5, \ldots\) form an A.P. and the second factors \(1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots\) form a G.P. with \(r = 2\), so this is an arithmetico-geometric series. Find the \(n\)th term, multiply \(S_n\) by \(r = 2\), subtract, and sum the G.P. that appears.

Step 1: \(n\)th term of the A.P. \(2, 3, 4, 5, \ldots\)
\[a_1 + (n - 1)d = 2 + (n - 1)(1)\]
\[= 2 + n - 1 = n + 1\]
Why: here \(a_1 = 2\) and \(d = 1\); this is the general term of an A.P.

Step 2: \(n\)th term of the G.P. \(1, 2, 2^{2}, 2^{3}, \ldots\)
\[a_1r^{n-1} = 1\cdot 2^{n-1} = 2^{n-1}\]
Why: first term 1, ratio 2. So the \(n\)th term of the series is \((n + 1)2^{n-1}\).

Step 3: Write \(S_n\)
\[S_n = 2\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 2 + 4\cdot 2^{2} + 5\cdot 2^{3}\]
\[+ \cdots + (n + 1)2^{n-1} \quad \text{(i)}\]
Why: the last term is the \(n\)th term from Steps 1 and 2.

Step 4: Multiply both sides by the common ratio 2 of the G.P.
The book prints: \(2S_n = 2\cdot 2 + 3\cdot 2^{2} + 4\cdot 2^{3} + 5\cdot 2^{4} + \ldots - (n)2^{n-1} + (n+1)2^{n}\)
With the correct sign:
\[2S_n = 2\cdot 2 + 3\cdot 2^{2} + 4\cdot 2^{3} + 5\cdot 2^{4}\]
\[+ \cdots + n\cdot 2^{n-1} + (n + 1)2^{n} \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: multiplying by 2 raises every power by one; each term is written under the term of (i) with the same power. The term with \(2^{n-1}\) is \(+\,n\cdot 2^{n-1}\) (2 times the \((n - 1)\)th term \(n\cdot 2^{n-2}\)); see the Book correction below.

Step 5: Subtract (ii) from (i)
\[S_n - 2S_n = 2\cdot 1 + (3 - 2)\cdot 2\]
\[+ (4 - 3)\cdot 2^{2} + (5 - 4)\cdot 2^{3}\]
\[+ \cdots + (n + 1 - n)2^{n-1}\]
\[- (n + 1)2^{n}\]
\[-S_n = 2\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 2 + 1\cdot 2^{2}\]
\[+ 1\cdot 2^{3} + \cdots + 1\cdot 2^{n-1}\]
\[- (n + 1)2^{n}\]
Why: terms with the same power differ only in their A.P. parts, and those differ by \(d = 1\). The first term of (i) and the last term of (ii) have no partner.

Step 6: Sum the G.P. in the braces
\[-S_n = 2 + \{2 + 2^{2} + 2^{3} + \cdots + 2^{n-1}\}\]
\[\quad - (n + 1)2^{n}\]
\[-S_n = 2 + \dfrac{2(2^{n-1} - 1)}{2 - 1}\]
\[\quad - (n + 1)\cdot 2^{n}\]
Why: \(2 + 2^{2} + \cdots + 2^{n-1}\) is a G.P. with first term 2, ratio 2 and \(n - 1\) terms; since \(r > 1\) we use \(\frac{a_1(r^{m} - 1)}{r - 1}\) with \(m = n - 1\).

Step 7: Simplify and solve for \(S_n\)
\[-S_n = 2 + 2^{n} - 2\]
\[\quad - n\cdot 2^{n} - 2^{n}\]
\[-S_n = -n\cdot 2^{n}\]
\[S_n = n\cdot 2^{n}\]
Why: \(2\cdot 2^{n-1} = 2^{n}\) and \((n + 1)2^{n} = n\cdot 2^{n} + 2^{n}\); then \(2 - 2\) and \(2^{n} - 2^{n}\) cancel. Multiply both sides by \(-1\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
1. The question prints the series as \(2\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 2 + 4\cdot 4 + 5\cdot 8 - \ldots\); the last sign should be \(+\) (the solution itself uses \(+\)).
2. Line (ii) prints \(\ldots - (n)2^{n-1} + (n+1)2^{n}\); the term with \(2^{n-1}\) is \(+\,n\cdot 2^{n-1}\), as the next line \((n + 1 - n)2^{n-1}\) shows.
The final answer \(S_n = n\cdot 2^{n}\) is correct.

blocks.title: Example 20
steps:
Given: the series \(3\cdot 1 + 4\cdot 2 + 5\cdot 2^{2} + 6\cdot 2^{3} + \ldots\)
To find: \(S_n\), the sum of the first \(n\) terms.
Method: as in Example 19: the A.P. part is \(3, 4, 5, 6, \ldots\) and the G.P. part is \(1, 2, 2^{2}, \ldots\) with \(r = 2\). Find the \(n\)th term, multiply by 2, subtract, sum the G.P. Several printed lines of this example have errors; they are shown and corrected below.

Step 1: \(n\)th terms of the A.P. and the G.P.
\[3 + (n - 1)(1) = 3 + n - 1 = n + 2\]
\[a_1r^{n-1} = 1(2)^{n-1} = 2^{n-1}\]
Why: A.P.: \(a_1 = 3\), \(d = 1\); G.P.: first term 1, ratio 2. So the \(n\)th term of the series is \((n + 2)2^{n-1}\).

Step 2: Write \(S_n\)
The book prints the first line as \(S_n = 3\cdot 1 + 4\cdot 2 + 5\cdot 2^{2} - 6\cdot 2^{3}, \ldots\) and line (i) as \(S_n = 3\cdot 1 + 4\cdot 2 + 5\cdot 2^{2} + 6\cdot 2^{3} + \ldots + (n+1)2^{n-1}\).
Correct line (i):
\[S_n = 3\cdot 1 + 4\cdot 2 + 5\cdot 2^{2} + 6\cdot 2^{3}\]
\[+ \cdots + (n + 2)2^{n-1} \quad \text{(i)}\]
Why: the \(n\)th term is \((n + 2)2^{n-1}\) (Step 1), and all signs are \(+\). Check with \(n = 1\): \(3\cdot 2^{0} = 3\cdot 1\).

Step 3: Multiply both sides by the common ratio 2
The book prints: \(2S_n = 3\cdot 2 + 4\cdot 2^{2} + 5\cdot 2^{3} + \ldots + (n+1)2^{n-1} + (n+1)2^{n}\)
Correct line (ii):
\[2S_n = 3\cdot 2 + 4\cdot 2^{2} + 5\cdot 2^{3} + \cdots\]
\[+ (n + 1)2^{n-1} + (n + 2)2^{n} \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: each power rises by one. The second last term is 2 times the \((n - 1)\)th term \((n + 1)2^{n-2}\), and the last term is 2 times \((n + 2)2^{n-1}\).

Step 4: Subtract (ii) from (i)
The book prints the first term as \(S_n - 2S_n = 3\cdot 2 + (4 - 3)\cdot 2 + (5 - 4)\cdot 2^{2} + \ldots\). The first term of (i) is \(3\cdot 1\):
\[S_n - 2S_n = 3\cdot 1 + (4 - 3)\cdot 2\]
\[+ (5 - 4)\cdot 2^{2} + (6 - 5)\cdot 2^{3}\]
\[+ \cdots + (n + 2 - n - 1)2^{n-1}\]
\[- (n + 2)2^{n}\]
\[-S_n = 3\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 2 + 1\cdot 2^{2} + 1\cdot 2^{3}\]
\[+ \cdots + 1\cdot 2^{n-1} - (n + 2)2^{n}\]
Why: terms with the same power differ by \(d = 1\) in their A.P. parts, including \((n + 2) - (n + 1) = 1\). The first term of (i) and the last term of (ii) have no partner.

Step 5: Sum the G.P. in the braces
The book prints this line as \(S_n = 3 + \{2 - 2^{2} + .2^{3} + \ldots + 2^{n-1}\}\ (n+1)2^{n}\). The correct line and the next step:
\[-S_n = 3 + \{2 + 2^{2} + 2^{3} + \cdots + 2^{n-1}\}\]
\[\quad - (n + 2)2^{n}\]
\[-S_n = 3 + \dfrac{2(2^{n-1} - 1)}{2 - 1}\]
\[\quad - (n + 2)2^{n}\]
Why: the left side is \(-S_n\), all signs in the braces are \(+\), and the last term is \((n + 2)2^{n}\). The braces hold a G.P. with first term 2, ratio 2 and \(n - 1\) terms.

Check:
\(n = 1\): \(-1 + 2\cdot 2 = 3\).
\(n = 2\): \(-1 + 3\cdot 4 = 11 = 3 + 8\).
\(n = 3\): \(-1 + 4\cdot 8 = 31 = 3 + 8 + 20\).
All agree; the book's final answer is correct.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The \(n\)th term is \((n + 2)2^{n-1}\), but several printed lines use \((n + 1)\) or wrong signs:
1. 'Let' line: \(5\cdot 2^{2} - 6\cdot 2^{3}, \ldots\) should be \(5\cdot 2^{2} + 6\cdot 2^{3} + \ldots\)
2. Line (i) ends \((n+1)2^{n-1}\); it should end \((n + 2)2^{n-1}\).
3. Line (ii) ends \((n+1)2^{n-1} + (n+1)2^{n}\); it should end \((n + 1)2^{n-1} + (n + 2)2^{n}\).
4. The subtraction starts \(3\cdot 2\); it should start \(3\cdot 1\).
5. The third line prints \(S_n = 3 + \{2 - 2^{2} + .2^{3} + \ldots + 2^{n-1}\}\ (n+1)2^{n}\); it should be \(-S_n = 3 + \{2 + 2^{2} + 2^{3} + \cdots + 2^{n-1}\} - (n + 2)2^{n}\).
The later lines use \((n + 2)\) correctly and the final answer \(S_n = -1 + (n + 1)2^{n}\) is correct.

blocks.title: Example 21
steps:
Given: the series \(2 + \frac{4}{3} + \frac{6}{9} + \frac{8}{27} + \ldots\)
To find: \(S_n\), the sum of the first \(n\) terms.
Method: each term is (A.P. term) \(\times\) (G.P. term): numerators \(2, 4, 6, 8, \ldots\) form an A.P., and \(1, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{9}, \frac{1}{27}, \ldots\) form a G.P. with \(r = \frac{1}{3}\). Multiply \(S_n\) by \(\frac{1}{3}\), subtract, and sum the G.P.

Step 1: \(n\)th terms of the A.P. and the G.P.
\[2 + (n - 1)(2) = 2 + 2n - 2 = 2n\]
\[(1)\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1} = \tfrac{1}{3^{n-1}}\]
Why: A.P.: \(a_1 = 2\), \(d = 2\); G.P.: first term 1, ratio \(\frac{1}{3}\). The \(n\)th term is \(\frac{2n}{3^{n-1}}\).

Step 2: Write \(S_n\) and \(\frac{1}{3}S_n\)
\[S_n = 2 + \tfrac{4}{3} + \tfrac{6}{9} + \tfrac{8}{27}\]
\[+ \cdots + \tfrac{2n}{3^{n-1}} \quad \text{(i)}\]
\[\tfrac{1}{3}S_n = \tfrac{2}{3} + \tfrac{4}{9} + \tfrac{6}{27} + \cdots\]
\[+ \tfrac{2n - 2}{3^{n-1}} + \tfrac{2n}{3^{n}} \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: multiplying by \(\frac{1}{3}\) raises each power of 3 in the denominators by one; terms with the same denominator are written under each other. The second last term of (ii) is \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the \((n - 1)\)th term \(\frac{2(n - 1)}{3^{n-2}}\).

Step 3: Subtract (ii) from (i)
\[\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{3}\right)S_n = 2 + \tfrac{4 - 2}{3} + \tfrac{6 - 4}{9}\]
\[+ \tfrac{8 - 6}{27} + \cdots\]
\[+ \tfrac{2n - 2n + 2}{3^{n-1}} - \tfrac{2n}{3^{n}}\]
\[\tfrac{2}{3}S_n = 2 + \left[\tfrac{2}{3} + \tfrac{2}{9} + \tfrac{2}{27}\right.\]
\[\left. + \cdots + \tfrac{2}{3^{n-1}}\right]\]
\[\quad - \tfrac{2n}{3^{n}}\]
Why: numerators over the same denominator differ by \(d = 2\); and \(1 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}\).

Step 4: Sum the G.P. in the brackets
\[\tfrac{2}{3}S_n = 2 + \dfrac{\frac{2}{3}\left\{1 - \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}\right\}}{1 - \frac{1}{3}}\]
\[\quad - \dfrac{2n}{3^{n}}\]
\[= 2 + \dfrac{\frac{2}{3}\left\{1 - \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}\right\}}{\frac{2}{3}}\]
\[\quad - \dfrac{2n}{3^{n}}\]
\[= 2 + 1 - \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1} - 2n\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n}\]
Why: the brackets hold a G.P. with first term \(\frac{2}{3}\), ratio \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(n - 1\) terms; \(r < 1\), so we use \(\frac{a_1(1 - r^{m})}{1 - r}\). The \(\frac{2}{3}\) cancels, and \(\frac{2n}{3^{n}} = 2n\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n}\).

Step 5: Solve for \(S_n\)
\[\tfrac{2}{3}S_n = 3 - \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1} - 2n\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n}\]
\[S_n = \tfrac{9}{2} - \tfrac{3}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1} - 3n\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n}\]
Why: \(2 + 1 = 3\); multiply every term by \(\frac{3}{2}\): \(3\cdot\frac{3}{2} = \frac{9}{2}\) and \(2n\cdot\frac{3}{2} = 3n\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Link with \(S_{\infty}\): here \(|r| = \frac{1}{3} < 1\), so as \(n \to \infty\) the answer tends to \(\frac{9}{2}\). The formula gives the same with \(a = 2, d = 2, b = 1, r = \frac{1}{3}\):
\[S_{\infty} = \dfrac{2}{\frac{2}{3}} + \dfrac{2\cdot\frac{1}{3}}{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2}} = 3 + \tfrac{3}{2} = \tfrac{9}{2}\]

blocks.title: Example 22
blocks.problem: Find the sum to \(n\) terms of the series: \(1 + 2x + 3x^{2} + 4x^{3} + \ldots\) where \(x \ne 1\). If \(|x| < 1\), sum the series to infinity.
steps:
Given: the series \(1 + 2x + 3x^{2} + 4x^{3} + \ldots\), \(x \ne 1\).
To find: (a) \(S_n\); (b) \(S_{\infty}\) when \(|x| < 1\).
Method: the coefficients \(1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots\) form an A.P. (\(d = 1\)) and \(1, x, x^{2}, \ldots\) a G.P. with ratio \(x\). Multiply by \(x\), subtract, sum the G.P.; then let \(n \to \infty\).

Step 1: Write \(S_n\) and \(xS_n\)
\[S_n = 1 + 2x + 3x^{2} + 4x^{3} + \cdots\]
\[+ nx^{n-1} \quad \text{...(i)}\]
\[xS_n = x + 2x^{2} + 3x^{3} + \cdots\]
\[+ (n - 1)x^{n-1} + nx^{n} \quad \text{...(ii)}\]
Why: the \(n\)th term is \(n\cdot x^{n-1}\) (A.P. part \(n\), G.P. part \(x^{n-1}\)). Multiplying by \(x\) raises every power by one; like powers are written under each other.

Step 2: Subtract (ii) from (i) and sum the G.P.
\[(1 - x)S_n = 1 + x + x^{2} + x^{3}\]
\[+ \cdots + x^{n-1} - nx^{n}\]
\[= \dfrac{1(1 - x^{n})}{1 - x} - nx^{n}\]
Why: coefficients of like powers differ by 1. \(1 + x + \cdots + x^{n-1}\) is a G.P. with first term 1, ratio \(x\) and \(n\) terms (powers 0 to \(n - 1\)); \(x \ne 1\), so the formula applies.

Step 3: Combine into one fraction and solve for \(S_n\)
\[= \dfrac{1 - x^{n} - n(1 - x)x^{n}}{1 - x}\]
\[= \dfrac{1 - x^{n} - nx^{n} + nx^{n+1}}{1 - x}\]
\[(1 - x)S_n = \dfrac{1 - (n + 1)x^{n} + nx^{n+1}}{1 - x}\]
\[S_n = \dfrac{1 - (n + 1)x^{n} + nx^{n+1}}{(1 - x)^{2}}\]
Why: write \(nx^{n} = \frac{n(1 - x)x^{n}}{1 - x}\) to get a common denominator; \(-n(1 - x)x^{n} = -nx^{n} + nx^{n+1}\) and \(-x^{n} - nx^{n} = -(n + 1)x^{n}\). Dividing by \(1 - x\) gives \((1 - x)^{2}\).

Step 4: Sum to infinity when \(|x| < 1\)
If \(|x| < 1\), then \(x^{n} \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).
\[S_{\infty} = \dfrac{1}{(1 - x)^{2}}\]
Why: both \((n + 1)x^{n}\) and \(nx^{n+1}\) tend to 0, because for \(|x| < 1\) not only \(x^{n} \to 0\) but also \(nx^{n} \to 0\) (stated at the start of 6.8.2). Only 1 is left in the numerator.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. If \(|r| < 1\): \(S_{\infty} = \frac{ab}{1 - r} + \frac{dbr}{(1 - r)^{2}}\).
2. Method for any A.G.P.: \(n\)th term, \(S_n\), multiply by \(r\), subtract, sum the middle G.P. (\(n - 1\) or \(n\) terms: count them).
3. The left side after subtracting is \((1 - r)S_n\): \(-S_n\) for \(r = 2\), \(\frac{2}{3}S_n\) for \(r = \frac{1}{3}\).
4. Always check the answer with \(n = 1\) and \(n = 2\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using \(S_{\infty}\) when \(|r| \ge 1\) (Examples 19 and 20 have \(r = 2\): no sum to infinity).
2. Forgetting the minus sign on the last term after subtracting.
3. Wrong number of terms in the middle G.P.: \(2 + \cdots + 2^{n-1}\) has \(n - 1\) terms; \(1 + x + \cdots + x^{n-1}\) has \(n\).
4. Leaving \(-S_n\) on the left and forgetting to multiply by \(-1\) at the end.
